title: The AI demo went perfectly. Then everything fell apart.
author: KeithGPT
selftext:
There's this brutal pattern I keep seeing in the AI startup world where a team nails the demo, gets the room excited, maybe even closes the deal... and then spends the next six months slowly realizing the thing doesn't actually work in production. Not because they were lying or even overpromising. But because demos are a completely different beast than deployment, and most teams don't treat them that way until it's too late.

The demo environment is basically a controlled lab. Real data is messy, user behavior is unpredictable, edge cases multiply fast, and the latency that felt acceptable in a 20 minute pitch becomes a dealbreaker when someone's using it 40 times a day. I think a lot of founders genuinely believe that getting the demo right means the hard part is done. It's actually the opposite. The demo is almost the easy part.

What I've noticed is that the teams who survive this phase are the ones who deliberately stress test before they ever show it to anyone. They treat the demo like a hypothesis, not a finished product. And they're honest with early customers about what's real versus what's roadmap. That transparency sounds risky but it tends to build more trust than overselling ever does.

I went deep on this exact topic in a recent conversation on Liftoff with Keith, specifically what causes AI projects to stall out after that initial excitement and what founders can do differently from the start.

comments.author: Am_Biyori
comments.body: sorry for sounding stupid, but what do you mean by demo? I thought a demo was akin to a vertical slice, Something playable that gives a taste of what the complete game will be and already playtested at least a little.

replies.author: Mysterra
replies.body:
That's what demo used to mean. It was pretty hard to have a fully functional demo without 'the product' essentially existing in some form.  
These days you can vibecode arbitrary functionality and have a demo that fakes having a product, but underneath everything is highly specific to the demo and only the demo, so going past the demo involves rebuilding absolutely everything from the ground up.

replies.author: KeithGPT
replies.body: Yea - demo could be like a movie trailer style or overview or it could be a vertical slice that shows deeper level of play and integration. Demos vary but full product needs to really deliver while avoiding the obvious beta challenges

replies.author: Am_Biyori
replies.body: Thanks to you and OP for the definitions! The vocab on this game dev reddit is so different from the others that I sometimes have trouble following the conversation. The post makes way more sense knowing that for vibe-coders a demo can mean multiple things. Thanks again.

replies.body: There’s really no point in doing that tho because with slightly more effort you can get something maintainable and polished. That’s kinda like, the whole beauty of AI
